cases.title: Sukulu phosphate project: land signed over for 99 years and no titles issued
cases.place: Sukulu village, Osukuru and Rubongi sub-counties, Tororo District, Uganda
cases.point: Sukulu village, Tororo District (OpenStreetMap node 2229128058, through Nominatim). AidData's record 60236 links that same node and separately gives approximate coordinates of 0.623611, 34.153611, about 4 km to the south; the record places the site about 11 km outside Tororo town, 5 km along the Busia-Tororo road. The land complaints are reported across Osukuru and Rubongi sub-counties, so this point is an area, not the parcels taken.

lenders.name: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC)
lenders.role: AidData record 60236. A US$240 million project financing facility signed on 4 December 2015 with Guangzhou Dong Song Energy Group (U) Co., Limited, the company developing the site, with credit insurance from Sinosure. The proceeds were to part-finance a commercial contract with 23rd Metallurgical Construction Group Company Limited for the phosphate fertiliser plant. AidData records that ICBC withheld loan disbursements because of legal challenges facing the company, and that it notified the company in 2019 that it was withholding US$60 million, at least part of it the undisbursed balance of the loan, because of a new policy requiring ICBC to lower its overseas loan centralisation ratio. AidData also records the loan as part of a larger US$620 million investment in the Osukuru industrial complex, and that some sources put the full facility for the whole project at up to US$520 million. This is not a World Bank project and has no P-number.

cases.conditions: The credit went to the Chinese developer rather than to the Ugandan state, and its proceeds were to pay a Chinese contractor, 23rd Metallurgical Construction Group Company Limited (AidData record 60236). The Tororo District Council and the Government of Uganda accepted the company's application on condition that it compensate all persons living on the land and evict no one; Matooke Republic reported on 16 December 2016 that the company had defaulted on that condition.

companies.name: Guangzhou Dong Song Energy Group (U) Co., Limited
companies.role: Borrower and developer; held the exploration licence granted on 1 August 2013 and took the land under surface rights agreements (AidData record 60236; Oil in Uganda, 8 July 2016)
companies.desc: Ugandan subsidiary of a Guangzhou energy and minerals group, set up to build the Osukuru industrial complex: a phosphate fertiliser plant, a sulphuric acid plant, a steel mill, a rare earth plant and a 12 MW thermal power station (AidData record 60236).

companies.name: 23rd Metallurgical Construction Group Company Limited
companies.role: Contractor for the works the ICBC credit financed (AidData record 60236)

companies.name: ABMAK Associates
companies.role: Ugandan law firm that handled the land transaction for the company and defended the payments made (Oil in Uganda, 8 July 2016; CorpWatch, 8 July 2016)

cases.community: Guangzhou Dong Song Energy was awarded 26.5 square kilometres, and the planned development could displace as many as 12,000 people in 14 villages; the community dropped its opposition in exchange for land titles, and the company's lawyers said villagers were paid 30 million shillings (US$8,750) an acre for a 99-year lease (CorpWatch, 8 July 2016). Rose Tibita, one of the hundreds of residents affected in Osukuru and Rubongi sub-counties, was described as having been forced to sign a surface rights agreement without knowing the contents of the contract and as realising later that she had surrendered her land for 99 years. She said: "When I went in, they opened for me pieces of paper and said you sign here. I first hesitated and asked where the rest of the (project affected) people were, they told me if I don't want the money, I should get out, and if I don't sign my land would be taken by government for free." Vincent Matano said: "To my surprise, they have taken our money, our land and no land title has been given to any of us." Denis Kusasira, managing partner of ABMAK Associates, the law firm that handled the transaction, said people were told they could take money or be resettled and none chose resettlement, and that the rate of 30 million shillings an acre, with further compensation for crops and other developments on the land and a 30 per cent disturbance allowance, was commensurate with the 99-year lease. The lawyers said they believed they had done an "excellent" job of compensating the villagers; Kusasira said "We are not one hundred percent clean, but this ... should be a case study" and "Even when you do everything well, they [NGOs] will still find something to complain about." Henry Okwalanga said he had benefited and that the company built him a house in place of a grass-thatched hut (CorpWatch; Oil in Uganda, 8 July 2016, as summarised by the Business and Human Rights Centre). On 16 December 2016 Matooke Republic reported that over 4,600 families had waited more than a year for payment and that only 123 of 4,800 families had received any compensation payment; it gives both figures. Jackson Oryema said: "I don't believe that I can be treated like this in my own country and my own government can allow this it is very unfair and we should be compensated." Some families said they had been duped into signing leases for 99 years instead of the 21 years agreed, and that spousal consent requirements were not followed in all cases, with some forms allegedly pre-signed. A district official who declined to be named said compensation should have been done by August 2014 and that two years of inflation had cut the value of the money. Emmanuel Osuna, the Tororo district chairperson when the project started, said the investors should compensate landowners adequately at government approved rates. The Resident District Commissioner Martin Orochi said the claims were untrue, that the project area of the phosphates factory alone was 600 acres excluding the mining areas, that people who complained were using the land for perennial agriculture and did not own it so were not entitled to compensation, that they had agreed to leave after their crops matured and were going peacefully, and that anyone complaining was "just a fraudster" (Matooke Republic).
cases.displaced_note: No document counting people or households actually moved was found. CorpWatch's figure of as many as 12,000 people in 14 villages is the reach of the awarded area, not a count of people moved. Matooke Republic's figures count families awaiting payment: 123 of 4,800 paid as of 16 December 2016, in an article that also says over 4,600 families.
cases.outcome: The fertiliser plant was commissioned on 24 October 2018 and produced 50,000 tonnes of bio-organic fertiliser, distributed to tea, sugarcane and other commercial farms for one planting season as a test. Commercial production was expected to start in January 2020 but was halted by a legal dispute over alleged fraudulent acquisition and ownership of the mineral deposit, which led to the cancellation of the company's mining lease, and ICBC withheld disbursements (AidData record 60236). No later record was found of land titles being issued to the families who signed the surface rights agreements.

cases.confidence_note: The land complaints come from three sources outside the lender: a Ugandan reporter for Oil in Uganda, a Ugandan weekly and CorpWatch, with the company's lawyers answering in two of them. The compensation rate of 30 million shillings an acre is the company's lawyers' own figure, and the lawyers say the compensation was commensurate with the lease. One article gives two totals for the families involved, over 4,600 and 4,800, and does not explain the gap. The Resident District Commissioner denies the claims and says those complaining did not own the land. Oil in Uganda's own page was reached only through the Business and Human Rights Centre's summary of it. The ICBC credit paid for the fertiliser plant contract, which the Resident District Commissioner puts at 600 acres excluding the mining areas, while the land complaints run across the 26.5 square kilometres awarded for the whole complex; the borrower is the company that took all of it, and AidData records the loan as part of a larger US$620 million investment in that complex. A district official said compensation should have been done by August 2014, before the loan was signed on 4 December 2015; what is recorded during and after the loan is that the payments and the titles had still not been made.
cx: Sukulu phosphate land leases and unpaid compensation
cases.ecosystem: The deposit at Sukulu was surveyed for minerals in 2008 by the Madhvani family, who announced an estimated 206 million tonnes; in late 2014 the government signed instead with Guangzhou Dong Song Energy, which was awarded 26.5 square kilometres of it for phosphate and rare earths (CorpWatch, 8 July 2016).
cases.whole: The company said the complex would create at least 1,000 jobs and produce 300,000 tonnes of phosphate fertiliser and 300,000 tonnes of steel a year, with revenue of about 1.6 trillion Ugandan shillings a year (CorpWatch, 8 July 2016). The plant produced one trial batch of 50,000 tonnes of bio-organic fertiliser after commissioning in October 2018 and then stopped (AidData record 60236). No independent production figure was found.

cases.title: SGR Phase 1 at Miritini: land acquired and four allottees left without land or payment
cases.point: Miritini, Jomvu Kuu ward, Mombasa (OpenStreetMap node 44927918, through Nominatim). The land is part of plot MN/VI/4805 and the parcels in dispute are numbers 3912 and 3913/VI/MN; the court records give no coordinate, so the point is the suburb.

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: AidData records 37103 and 31777. Two loan agreements signed with Kenya's National Treasury on 11 May 2014 for Phase 1 of the Standard Gauge Railway: a buyer's credit of US$2,003,584,028.87, later revised to US$1,903,404,827.42, at 6-month Libor plus 3.6 per cent with a 15.25-year maturity and insurance from Sinosure; and a preferential buyer's credit of US$1.6 billion at 2 per cent with a 20.25-year maturity. The proceeds were on-lent to Kenya Railways Corporation to pay 90 per cent of two contracts with China Road and Bridge Corporation. This is not a World Bank project and has no P-number.

cases.conditions: Repayment was secured on project revenue held in escrow, with minimum balances set by a 2014 escrow account agreement, and on a take-or-pay freight agreement under which the Kenya Ports Authority had to consign a minimum volume of cargo to the railway or make good the shortfall; a 1.5 per cent Railway Development Levy on imports was set up to cover any gap and the government's own share of the cost. The loans financed 90 per cent of the two commercial contracts with China Road and Bridge Corporation, with the remaining 10 per cent to be paid by Kenya Railways as counterpart financing; the same AidData record elsewhere describes the Kenyan government's portion of the commercial contract cost as 15 per cent, and does not reconcile the two (AidData records 37103 and 31777). Land acquisition and compensation were the Kenyan state's responsibility, carried out by the National Land Commission.

companies.name: National Land Commission
companies.role: The Kenyan state body that compulsorily acquired the land and refused to pay the four allottees (Court of Appeal, Civil Application 10 of 2020)
companies.desc: Independent commission created by Kenya's 2010 constitution to manage public land on behalf of the national and county governments and to carry out compulsory acquisition and pay compensation under the Land Act.

companies.name: China Road and Bridge Corporation
companies.role: Builder of the Mombasa-Nairobi line under the two contracts the loans financed (AidData record 37103)

companies.name: Kenya Railways Corporation
companies.role: State railway that borrowed the proceeds and supervised the works (AidData record 37103)

companies.name: Miritini Free Port Limited
companies.role: Registered owner of the plot, which received the compensation for the acquisition (Court of Appeal, Civil Application 10 of 2020)

cases.community: The National Land Commission compulsorily acquired 22.11 hectares of plot MN/VI/4805 for the Mombasa-Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway and paid the registered owner, Miritini Free Port Limited. The Court of Appeal ruling of 20 November 2020 gives the sum paid as Kshs 1,475,486,845; the High Court judgment of 12 November 2019, an earlier High Court ruling of 23 July 2018 and a Court of Appeal ruling of 25 October 2024 give it as Kshs 1,475,486,485, with a further interruption award of Kshs 360,000,000. The 2024 ruling records that the public was informed in January 2015 that the Government of Kenya intended to acquire the 22.11 hectares. Theresia Runji, Marieta Gitonga Chege, Naomi Kiio and Sammy Macharia Kara, who had been issued with letters of allotment for the land in 2000, filed Mombasa Constitutional Petition No. 17 of 2018, and the commission denied their claim; their petition said the allotment followed an eviction of the petitioners and others from parcels at Bombolulu. On 12 November 2019 Justice Eric Ogola held that the commission had abused its statutory powers in refusing to compensate the four, that its decision was unconstitutional because they were never heard, that it amounted to abuse of office because it was reached in disregard of the commission's own previous findings, and that they had not been served with notice of the government's intention to acquire the land. He directed the commission to tabulate, assess and compensate the value of parcels 3912 and 3913/VI/MN, the disputed part of the plot, as at the date of acquisition plus interest at commercial rates, and said: "My understanding is that this money has already been disbursed and the petitioners left without land. Justice demands that the petitioners be justly and promptly compensated for the loss of their land." He also held they were entitled to damages, and that the registration of the disputed part under Miqdad Enterprises was illegal because it was done in violation of an order. Their lawyer Gikandi Ngibuini argued their right to prompt and full compensation had been infringed, exposing them to economic hardships, losses and damages. The commission argued they had produced no evidence that the land was subject to compulsory acquisition; Miritini Free Port called the petition an abuse of the court's due process; the judge noted unchallenged evidence that Miritini Free Port remained the registered owner of the undisputed part of the land, that there was no dispute over that part, so the commission's decision of 1 December 2015 was unchallenged as it related to it, and said the judgment covered only the two parcels claimed (Daily Nation, 2 December 2019; Court of Appeal, Civil Application 10 of 2020; High Court, Constitutional Petition 17 of 2018).
cases.displaced_note: No document counting people moved for this section was found. The court records four allottees left without the land and without payment.
cases.outcome: The railway was completed on 31 May 2017 (AidData record 37103). The commission went to the Court of Appeal at Mombasa, which ruled on its application on 20 November 2020 (Civil Application 10 of 2020) and gave further rulings in Civil Appeal (Application) No. 24 of 2020 on 5 November 2021 and 25 October 2024. The Court of Appeal granted an order of stay of execution of the 12 November 2019 judgment, recorded in a High Court ruling of 25 October 2024 as "an order of stay of execution of the judgment herein issued by the Court of Appeal". A further High Court ruling of 20 February 2026 in the same petition states that "the orders for stay of execution of the judgment have not been varied" or reviewed and that to execute the judgment "would be an exercise in futility". No record of payment to the four was found.

cases.confidence_note: The harm sits in Kenya's published court record and in a Kenyan newspaper's report of the judgment, both outside the lender. The sum paid to the registered owner is given two ways in that record: Kshs 1,475,486,845 in the Court of Appeal ruling of 20 November 2020 and Kshs 1,475,486,485 in the High Court judgment of 12 November 2019 and in two other rulings; no document explains the difference. The Daily Nation reports the same awards as "Sh1.4 billion and another Sh360,000", where the court records give a further interruption award of Kshs 360,000,000. The spelling of the petitioners' names varies within the court record itself, which carries Theresia Runji and Theresa Runji, Naomi Kiio and Naomi Kio, and Sammy M. Kara and Sammy Macharia Kara; the Daily Nation's shorter forms are those variants and not a separate account. The Daily Nation of 2 December 2019 reports the ruling as made "on Monday", while the court record dates the judgment 12 November 2019. The judgments were read through kenyalaw.org's own search index, which returns each document's title, court, date and matching passages but not its full text, because kenyalaw.org's judgment pages answer an automated request with an Amazon Web Services firewall challenge; judy.legal publishes only the opening of the 20 November 2020 ruling without a subscription. The result of each appellate ruling is therefore not stated here. The record also describes the four as squatters who had not benefited from any squatters settlement scheme, which matches the petition's account of an allotment made after an eviction at Bombolulu. Land acquisition and compensation were the Kenyan state's responsibility and were paid from Kenyan funds; the China Eximbank loans financed 90 per cent of the two construction contracts.
cx: Standard Gauge Railway Phase 1 land acquisition at Miritini
cases.whole: The line from Mombasa to Nairobi opened on 31 May 2017, eighteen months ahead of schedule, and was the largest infrastructure project built in Kenya since independence; AidData's project description gives its length as 485 km and its location note as 475 km. In 2018 Kenya's Department of Public Prosecutions named the chairman of the National Land Commission, Mohammed Abdalla Swazuri, and the managing director of Kenya Railways Corporation, Atanas Kariuki Maina, among 18 officials, businesspeople and companies arrested on suspicion of corruption over land allocation for the railway, in an investigation centred on allegations that officials siphoned taxpayer money through compensation claims for land used for the railway (Reuters, quoted in AidData record 37103). A report by Kenya's transport ministry tabled in parliament in 2018 said the railway lost KES 9.8 billion (US$90.3 million) in its first year; a 2020 ministry report said it lost US$200 million over three years, on revenue of US$230.7 million against operating costs of US$430.5 million. In July 2022 Kenya received overdue repayment notices from China Eximbank, and in October 2022 local media reported a default and a default interest charge of US$10.8 million, or 1.312 billion Kenyan shillings (AidData record 37103).

cases.title: Kibwezi-Mutomo-Kitui road: land and shops taken and compensation unpaid since 2017
cases.place: Kitui town and the Kibwezi-Migwani road, Kitui and Makueni Counties, Kenya
cases.point: Kitui town, where those affected demonstrated outside the county commissioner's office in March 2022 and from where a senator took a delegation to the National Land Commission (OpenStreetMap node 44933078, through Nominatim). The road runs from the A8 junction near Kibwezi north through Ikutha, Mutomo, Kitui and Kabati to Migwani, so this point is one place along it.

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: AidData records 53111 and 58152. A buyer's credit agreement signed with the Government of Kenya on 29 November 2016 covering 85 per cent of commercial contracts worth KES 50 billion for three sections totalling 472 km; AidData estimates the face value at US$418,578,082.97 and records that none of its sources states the dollar face value. Phase 1, 192 km worth KES 23 billion, is recorded separately as record 58152 at US$194.7 million. AidData also notes that Kenya's project monitoring system lists two loans for this road, of US$212.8 million and US$206,134,747.16, and that it is unclear whether these refer to different projects. Terms: 15-year maturity, 3 per cent interest. The loan identification number in Kenya's external public debt register is 2016052. This is not a World Bank project and has no P-number.

cases.conditions: The credit paid 85 per cent of the cost of commercial contracts held by a Chinese contractor, China Hydropower International Co., Ltd, with the Kenyan side covering the rest (AidData record 53111). Land acquisition and compensation were the Kenyan state's responsibility, through the National Land Commission.

companies.name: China Hydropower International Co., Ltd (Sinohydro)
companies.role: Contractor for the works the credit financed (AidData record 53111); The Star names Sinohydro Corporation as the firm that built the road

companies.name: Kenya National Highways Authority
companies.role: State roads authority that administered the project (AidData record 53111)
companies.desc: National agency under Kenya's roads ministry responsible for the management, development and maintenance of class A, B and C national trunk roads.

companies.name: National Land Commission
companies.role: The state body that made and then, according to a Senate record, revised downwards the compensation awards (Kenyan Senate Hansard record of Senator Enoch Kiio Wambua)
companies.desc: Independent commission created by Kenya's 2010 constitution to manage public land and to carry out compulsory acquisition and pay compensation under the Land Act.

cases.community: On 6 December 2020 The Star reported that about 5,000 land owners had not been paid for land taken for the tarmacking of the 172 km Kibwezi-Kitui-Migwani road. Their spokesman Michael Kivoto said people had been allocated land by the defunct Kitui County Council and had put up shops and other structures for income, "only for the buildings to be brought down without anyone talking of compensation", that some had gone to court while most could not afford lawyers' fees, and that some of those affected had sunk into depression; a delegation of 26 people took the matter to Kalonzo Musyoka. On 4 March 2022 The Star reported that the project "displaced about 5,000 persons who either lost their land, homes and business premises", that they were asking for Sh1.6 billion and had not been fully compensated five years after work began, and that they demonstrated outside the Kitui county commissioner's office on 3 March 2022. Joseph Wambua said: "We lost property such as houses and farms which were our source of livelihood. Life is tough and the government should stop the delays and pay up." Kanini Kitili said she had lost a big chunk of land and that it was unfair for the government to pay the contractor while no one cared about the displaced. The deputy county commissioner Dorcas Rono said the authorities would follow up the issue. In March 2023 the Member for Kibwezi West, Mwengi Mutuse, asked the Cabinet Secretary for Lands to explain the delay in paying people whose land was compulsorily acquired for the road in 2017 and to say whether the commission would review the compensation upwards given the delay; Parliament's record of the question shows no response. The Star, reporting the question on 21 March 2023, said the commission was to compensate about 5,000 title owners who were relocated for the project and that the families had been pushed out and were wallowing in poverty. A Kenyan Senate record carries Senator Enoch Kiio Wambua saying that officers from the National Land Commission were reviewing awards downwards by a wide margin two months after people had been given an award, that compensation, pollution and the companies' community obligations on this section were all serious, and that he had led a delegation of affected people from Kitui Township to the commission. Landowners also went to court over the acquisition. Twenty-two plaintiffs sued the National Land Commission and Sinohydro in the Environment and Land Court, seeking an injunction restraining the defendants, in a case recording that the suit land was being taken to construct the road (Daniel Muema Joel & 21 others v National Land Commission & 2 others, Case No. 47 of 2018, ruling of 20 September 2019). Ravaspaul Kyalo Mutisya sued the commission in the same court over a building that was under construction and land excavated to build the road, which the ruling records was to be part of the land the commission was to acquire for it (ruling of 8 March 2022). Three plaintiffs appealed against the Kenya National Highways Authority over their properties taken by compulsory acquisition for the road (Kitheka & 2 others v Kenya National Highways Authority, Environment and Land Appeal 38 of 2021, ruling of 22 July 2024). Fifty-six petitioners took the commission to Kenya's Land Acquisition Tribunal over parcels said to be required for the road (Mulu & 55 others v National Land Commission & 2 others, Land Acquisition Petition E038 of 2024, judgment of 2 December 2025).
cases.displaced_note: The figure of about 5,000 is described three ways in three reports and is not a count of people moved: "about 5,000 land owners" not compensated (The Star, 6 December 2020), "about 5,000 persons who either lost their land, homes and business premises" (The Star, 4 March 2022), and "about 5,000 title owners who were relocated" (The Star, 21 March 2023). No document counting households actually relocated was found.
cases.outcome: The road was completed in May 2022 (The Star, 21 March 2023). The 2023 parliamentary question on the delay has no answer recorded in Parliament's own record of it. Claims over the acquisition of land for the road were still before Kenya's Land Acquisition Tribunal in December 2025. No record of payment was found.

cases.confidence_note: The unpaid compensation is carried by a Kenyan newspaper in three reports across 2020, 2022 and 2023, by a parliamentary question whose own record shows no answer, by a Senate speech, and by Kenyan court and tribunal records running from 2018 to 2025, all outside the lender. The figure of about 5,000 comes from that one newspaper and is described differently each time. The Star of 21 March 2023 calls the questioner the Kibwezi East MP while Parliament's record of the question gives the Member for Kibwezi West. The Senate record carried here gives no sitting date, so none is stated, and the senator declared an interest in the matter as a senator from Kitui County, where the longest section of the road runs. The downward revision of awards rests on that single Senate speech. The amount claimed, Sh1.6 billion, is what those affected asked for, not an assessed figure. The court and tribunal records were read through kenyalaw.org's own search index, which returns each document's title, court, date and matching passages but not its full text, because kenyalaw.org's judgment pages answer an automated request with an Amazon Web Services firewall challenge; no outcome is stated here for any of those proceedings. The Star gives the road's length as 172 km and AidData gives Phase 1 as 192 km of a 472 km three-section project. The Star says the project was launched by President Kenyatta in 2017 and AidData says construction began on 6 December 2016.
cx: Kibwezi-Mutomo-Kitui road land acquisition and unpaid compensation
cases.whole: The road is part of the Mombasa-Isiolo-Moyale corridor and gives a direct link between Mombasa and Ethiopia; it is used by buses, matatus and trucks heading for Embu, Kiambu, Kitui, Machakos, Makueni, Meru and Mombasa, and cuts at least 100 km off long-distance trips (The Star, 21 March 2023). The project was 53 per cent complete in May 2019 against an original completion date of 15 February 2021, held up by land acquisition, the relocation of power lines along the corridor, late payments, a shortage of water for the works and a stoppage by the contractor after Covid-19 cases in Kitui; residents also complained of noise and dust from the works (AidData record 53111).
